ImageDescription.value:
How to spend your Christmas bonus?
1933 Rolls Royce Phanton II Continental 2 Door Sports Coupe. Coachwork by Gurney Nutting.

This magnificent Phantom II, chassis 67 MW is one of just 19 MW type chassis of the total 281 Continental Series series cars produced and is finished in its original midnight blue with contrasting light blue hide and dark blue wilton carpets. This majestically styled Phantom II Continental was sold out of Jack Barclays eponymous Rolls Royce and Bentley showroom in Berkeley Square in London to a Lady Irene Dunn from whence it made its way to the USA before returning to these shores in the 1950's. This is the only car to have been built to this unique design which incorporates a very light side window feature which make it extremely pleasant to drive and be driven in. Two spare wheels mounted at the rear complement the sporting art deco look. Restoration of 67 MW was begun in earnest in 1995 and finished in London in 1998, most of the work being carried out by Frank Dale and Stepsons' renowned Bentley and Rolls Royce workshop in Isleworth, West London for which there are

invoices on file. A considerable history file accompanies the car which is available for viewing by appointment in Kew. source

Categories.value: PD US|Media contributed by the Digital Public Library of America|Media contributed by University of Colorado Boulder Libraries|Artworks without Wikidata item|Media contributed by the Plains to Peaks Collective|Information field template with formatting|Offices in the 1890s|Desks in the United States|Digital Public Library of America files missing required SDC statements|PD-US missing SDC copyright status|Digital Public Library of America files missing creator|Typewriters in the United States

ImageDescription.value: photographic paper photography (process) This is one of the most interesting pictures in the entire set. It shows James H. Baker's office, Room 108, on the NW corner of the main floor of Old Main in February 1893 showing very clearly what was needed to administer a university. This is one of the pictures JRB took for the University's display in the Columbian Exposition. The calendar is turned to February 1893 and is from the "Mutual Life Insurance Company" which is observing its "Semicentennial 1843-1893" and which is represented by "Richard A. McCurdy." Above the roll top desk across the room is a frame of 12 interior pictures of campus buildings. The top left looks like the chapel. The other top ones are the DeLong Math room (209) but the pictures are not from this set, i.e., 14-3 does not appear here. The frame at the right has 12 exterior pictures which are held in with thumb tacks but the pictures are warped and bowed. The views are easily identified from left to right, top to bottom, (Main in the distance, the President's house at right), (Old Main), (Univ. Lake), (Lake and President's house), (Main - identical with second one above), (construction of Woodbury - this is an earlier picture than on pg. 63 of Glory Colorado), (Woodbury), (the President's house and Main), (Cottage No. 1), (Cottage No. 2), (the Anatomy building), (the Medical building without its west wing). The frame over the desk is similar to the top center one in 14-6 and the frame at right is probably the one at lower left in 14-6. It is quite possible that these frames were taken from the President's office and had new pictures mounted in them for the Columbian Exposition of 14-6. The floor has carpet, the walls have wainscotting, like that in 14-5, and the ceiling has a spiral pattern wall paper. The door has a porcelain doorknob with a keyÂ¬lock below It and an eye for fastening it open below and to the right of the knob. The door has three large hinges and opens inward. There is a transom window but no hardware for adjusting it is visible. The top seems to be tipped outward toward the corridor. It seems odd that the occupant of the room could not adjust the transom from within the room. The four bulb light fixture is on a pipe from the ceiling. It may be adjustable in height by rotating the lower part causing the helical center pipe to screw into or out of the pipe above it. The globes are snapped on independently by a flat rotary knob like today's fixtures. The bulb at right is lighted. The heavy ornate center table has twin wheel casters on each foot. The feet are badly scarred and scratched. The top might be leatherÂ—pulled over the edges and anchored under the strips of wood. The typewriter says "Remington Standard Typewriter No. 2" across the base and it looks as though the carriage return arm is on the right! On the center of the table are a small book, two or three bottles of ink and two pens, while on the far corner is a big steel press probably for imprinting the seal of the University. The table has two locked drawers at the left. The far roll top desk is full of all sorts of papers and on the desk are a horizontal rack for holding pens, two glass inkwells, and a bowl with a sponge which is kept wet for sealing envelopes. Through the door at the left is the outer office (Room 109). A book and box are on the table, a coat and derby hat are on hooks on the long coat rack on the wall. The outer office may not be carpeted. On the wall to the left of the door is "Nell's Topographical (?) Map of the State of Colorado" which Is indicative of a period in which the President (Baker) and the University had a very great concern for the people and the State which he and the University served. ImageDescription.value:
The Imperial Venue on West Green Road, Tottenham, London, England.
The Imperial opened on 6 November 1913 as the Imperial Electric Theatre (cinema), designed by architect E. A. Thorne, with 427 seats on a single ground level with a small foyer. The first screening was The Only Chance, starring Tom Mix. After closing during the First World War, it re-opened as the Imperial Cinema, run by the Lion Cinematograph Company Ltd. By 1931, then operated by H. & G. Sado, it had been fitted with a Western Electric sound system, reflecting the transition to 'talkies.' In 1945, it was taken over by Newcastle-upon-Tyne based Essoldo Circuit cinemas and became known as the Essoldo Cinema, with 550 seats, with a CinemaScope screen installed in 1954. However, the cinema closed on 31 May 1958, its final double-feature being Tyrone Power in Billy Wilder's 1957 film Witness For the Prosecution and Philip Friend in the Ernest Morris 1957 The Betrayal. After closure the cinema became a carpet store until 2000, selling surplus end of rolls. The building then stood empty until 2004, when it became a church keeping much of the interior. In 2017 the building was converted to a banqueting hall, with the current name The Imperial Venue, being used for events and catering. The building, at 290–294 West Green Road, is one of the relatively few early purpose-built cinemas in Tottenham to survive through the 20th century, even though many cinemas closed or were converted to other uses. In early days, locals called it "the Imp" or "the Flea Pit". It has retained much of its facade and some interior features.

ImageDescription.value:
West Green Road Tottenham London England, including The Imperial Venue.
The Imperial opened on 6 November 1913 as the Imperial Electric Theatre (cinema), designed by architect E. A. Thorne, with 427 seats on one level and a small foyer. The first screening was The Only Chance, starring Tom Mix. After closing during the First World War, it re-opened as the Imperial Cinema, run by the Lion Cinematograph Company Ltd. By 1931, then operated by H. & G. Sado, it had been fitted with a Western Electric sound system, reflecting the transition to 'talkies.' In 1945, it was taken over by Newcastle-upon-Tyne based Essoldo Circuit cinemas and became known as the Essoldo Cinema, with 550 seats, with a CinemaScope screen installed in 1954. However, the cinema closed on 31 May 1958, its final feature being Tyrone Power in Witness For the Prosecution and Phillip Friend in The Betrayal. After closure the cinema became a carpet store until 2000, selling surplus end of rolls. The building then stood empty until 2004, when it became a church keeping much of the interior. In 2017 the building was converted to a banqueting hall, with the current name The Imperial Venue, being used for events and catering. The building, at 290–294 West Green Road, is one of the relatively few early purpose-built cinemas in Tottenham to survive through the 20th century, even though many cinemas closed or were converted to other uses. Locals used to call it "the Imp" or "the Flea Pit" in early days. It has retained much of its facade and some interior features.

ImageDescription.value: How it used to be - in the 1980s, the first yoga mats used in the Iyengar Yoga tradition were cut from rolls of green rubber underlay meant for use under carpets. Angela Farmer started the use of these "sticky mats", and yoga teachers used to buy rolls of the stuff and sell six foot lengths at cost price to their students. This one was mine.
